newsitem.title: UK: Major revives trusty soapbox for election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Major revives trusty soapbox for election campaign.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major pulled out his trusty soap box on Monday to take his message to the people, just a few hours after calling an election for May 1.
Major returned to Luton, north of London, where he first used the battered soapbox as a makeshift stage during the 1992 campaign.
The soapbox, although mocked by journalists, was seen as a turning point in the Conservatives' campaign and took on mythical qualities when Major was re-elected against the odds.
With his party now lagging Labour by more than 20 points in opinion polls, Major is intent on repeating the soapbox effect.
He arrived in Luton to chaotic scenes, jostled and shouted at, as well as cheered, by a large crowd.

From the second he stepped out of his car, Major was met by a barrage of shouts about equally divided between supporters chanting slogans such as "five more years" and opponents shouting "five more weeks."
Eggs were thrown, but landed nowhere near him.

As soon as Major stood on the soapbox to give an impromptu speech in the middle of a small park, a crowd of protesters began chanting loudly "Major out" and "Tory Scum". But even his most vocal dissenters were good-humoured.
Major raised his voice loud enough to rise above the protesters and said they only showed the risks of voting for Labour.
"This is what we are fighting against," he said, a large smile on his face. "I want to let these people continue chanting because I want Britain to know what is coming out of the left wing."
No amount of "mindless slogans" would stop the Conservatives taking the campaign directly to the people of Britain in their bid to win an unprecedented fifth consecutive term, he said.
"I have no intention of being deterred by stunt demonstrations with stunt demonstrators who have no policies," he said.
"I have no shred of doubt that the five years to come will be five more Conservative years to carry on the revolution of the last 18 years."
At one point the crush was so great that the police seemed to lose control. There were unpleasant confrontations as officers forcibly shoved and pushed demonstrators out of the prime minister's way.
He appeared flustered at first but seemed to gain confidence as the surprise visit continued and kept smiling throughout.
"The last time I came to Luton I had a reception just like this and three weeks later we won both Luton seats and the general election," Major yelled from his tiny stage.
Conservatives hold both Luton seats, but with narrow majorities, and they represent the kind of seats that Labour has to conquer to win the election.
The town, 40 miles north of London, is dominated by the Vauxhall car factory and the fast-expanding airport.

Many local people prospered under the Conservatives' programme of selling public housing but the town has suffered badly under the economic recession and the collapse of the housing market in the early 1990s.
Many shops have closed down in the town centre, which has a depressed feel.
